content:
We've talked many times about the issue with USB-C cables: they all look pretty much the same, but their actual capabilities can vary enormously.

Google tackled this in Chrome OS years ago, and we suggested Apple do the same. It still hasn't, but now there's a free Mac app called WhatCable that turns your Mac into a hardware cable tester……

We buy almost every electronic device these days with a USB-C cable in the box, and it's easy to end up with a drawer full of them and no idea which to use when. Each one may have different maximum capabilities in each area:

  • Data transfer speed
  • Video bandwidth
  • Power delivery capability

The variation can be huge — a good cable may support 40Gb/s data, 8K 60Hz video, and 240W power; a poor one may be charge-only, or a low-speed cable limited to 480Mbps.

Hardware cable testers are sold, which can report the capabilities of the connected cable; now there's a free Mac app that does the same. WhatCable works by measuring the performance when the cable is in actual use, or by connecting it from one USB-C port on the Mac to another — like that joke about Macs charging themselves.

It can also read the identifying data from chips embedded in the cable to determine the manufacturer and whether it has USB-IF certification. Note that lack of certification doesn't necessarily mean it's counterfeit — it may simply be that the manufacturer chose not to pay for certification.

This works because the Mac already reads these capability data from embedded chips. WhatCable just makes it easy to access this data and translate it into plain English.

See whether the cable, the charger, or the Mac is limiting the current charging speed, and indicate the power delivery specification that has been negotiated. Get plain-English explanations of whether it's the Mac port, the cable, or the device that is slowing down the connection, so you know whether buying a faster cable would actually help. When connecting a display, see whether it's running at full resolution and refresh rate, or being limited, and whether the limitation is in the adapter, cable, or mode selected. From marked USB-C cables, decipher the cable speed, current rating, manufacturer identity, and USB PD capability marking.

The free version includes all of the above, while a Pro version offers more detailed data, like a real-time negotiation analysis of each connection, showing why two devices ended up operating at a particular charging or data speed. The Pro version is a one-time purchase of £9.99 (around $13.40).

The Verge's Sean Hollister tested it and found it worked well, though not perfectly, since some cables exaggerate their specs.
